findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.title: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite
findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Storybook: Missing origin validation in Storybook preview allows code injection from malicious websites
findings.summary:
**Summary:** A malicious website may be able to cause unauthorized file changes in a developer’s project while an affected Storybook development server is running. Under additional conditions, a changed file could be executed by a local runtime with the developer’s privileges. We are not aware of exploitation in the wild.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server in the affected versions.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server that you never open in a web browser (e.g. headless automation, MCP clients)
- You run or visit a built version of Storybook

Recent versions of Chrome and Firefox may ask for permission before a website can connect to a `localhost` service. This reduces the risk, but does not remove it. Do not grant this permission to websites you don’t trust.

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

- 11.0.0-alpha.6
- 10.6.2
- 9.1.21
- 8.6.19

### Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, we've added feature flags that can disable specific security updates to support your existing workflows.

Please carefully read the introduced flags and the consequences of using them.

findings.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.

The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.

No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any co

findings.title: Pillow: Heap use-after-free when encoding TIFF to an in-memory buffer
findings.summary:
### Summary
Saving an image as TIFF to an in-memory buffer can trigger a heap use-after-free if libtiff rejects a tag at encode time. When `TIFFWriteScanline` fails, the encoder frees its output buffer but leaves the libtiff handle open. Later, when the encoder object is torn down, `TIFFClose` flushes buffered bytes through the write callback and writes into the freed buffer. An application that re-encodes attacker-influenced images to TIFF in memory can be crashed and is a candidate for remote code execution.

### Details
The failure path in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` frees `clientstate->data` for the in-memory case but does not close the TIFF or null `clientstate->tiff` (the file-descriptor branch just above it does set `tiff = NULL`):

- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1041-1046`

Teardown then calls `ImagingLibTiffEncodeCleanup`, which runs `TIFFClose(tiff)` because `tiff` is still set:

- `src/encode.c:99-101`
- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:955`

`TIFFClose` flushes through `_tiffWriteProc`, which reallocs and memcpys into the freed `state->data`:

- `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103-115`

The Predictor tag is a convenient trigger: the floating-point predictor (value 3) is invalid for integer sample data, so libtiff aborts the write.

### PoC
```python
import io
from PIL import Image

# In-memory TIFF re-encode. libtiff rejects Predictor=3 (floating point) on integer
# data, so TIFFWriteScanline fails. The encoder frees clientstate->data but leaves the
# TIFF open; cleanup's TIFFClose then writes through the callback into the freed buffer.
im = Image.new("L", (64, 64))
buf = io.BytesIO()
im.save(buf, format="TIFF", compression="tiff_lzw", tiffinfo={317: 3})  # 317 = Predictor
```

Run it:
```
$ python 01_poc.py
PredictorSetup: Floating point "Predictor" not supported with 1 data format.
OSError: encoder error -2 when writing image file
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96` with libtiff. The process aborts during cleanup af

findings.title: Pillow: Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
Location: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216  in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's `Image.quantize(palette=...)`, the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary.

The bug is in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` in `src/libImaging/Palette.c`. It fills a local `UINT8 c[512]` only inside loops bounded by `palette->size`. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. `topalette()` in `src/libImaging/Convert.c` then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. `topalette()` rejects a `NULL` palette but not one with `size == 0`. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry `"P"` image: a PNG with a zero-length `PLTE` chunk opened with `Image.open()`, a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`. The attacker must control the *palette* image; the source image can be anything, and `RGB` sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. findings.title: Pillow: P;2L and P;4L decoders may read 1 to 3 bytes past the passed buffer size
findings.summary:
### Summary

On `main`, even with the guard in #9725, it's possible to have these decoders read 1 to 3 bytes past the end of the passed buffer with a suitable width/height.

### Details

`ImagingRawDecode` and the `P;2L` / `P;4L` unpackers disagree about how many bytes a line of data occupies.

The raw decoder derives the line size from the bits per pixel

```c
state->bytes = (state->xsize * state->bits + 7) / 8;
```

and uses it both for the bounds check and to advance to the next line. For `P;2L` and `P;4L`, `bits` is 2 and 4 respectively.

But these two rawmodes are not packed pixels but 2 or 4 *bit planes*, each padded to a whole number of bytes. `unpackP2L` computes `s = (pixels + 7) / 8` and reads plane *k* at offset `k * s`, and `unpackP4L` does the same across four planes. Their real footprint is therefore `planes * ((xsize + 7) / 8)`.

For some widths, padding each plane separately makes this footprint larger than `state->bytes`. For example, at width 1, the decoder accounts for one byte, while the unpackers read two or four bytes. The decoder accepts data that is too short for the last line and on the other hand advances to subsequent lines by less than a line, so every line after the first is also read from the wrong offset.

#9725's check is misshapen for this:

* It can reject data of the right length: 8x1 `P;2L` image is 2 bytes but is not accepted.
* It still accepts buffers shorter than the unpackers require for a given image shape.
* It measures the length with `len(data)`, which is an element count rather than a byte count; e.g. `memoryview(array("I", [0,0,0,0,0]))` (20 bytes) is rejected while `mv.tobytes()` is accepted.

### PoC ( `ghsa_p2l_p4l.py`)

```python
from array import array
from PIL import Image

# 1 byte past
Image.frombytes("P", (1, 4), array("B", [0] * 4), "raw", "P;2L")

# 3 bytes past
Image.frombytes("P", (1, 8), array("B", [0] * 8), "raw", "P;4L")
```
is the almost-simplest reproducer.

findings.title: Vitest: Servers misapply `server.fs.deny`, serving `.env`, private keys, `.git`, and the API token file
findings.summary:
### Summary

In Vitest 5, Vite's `server.fs.deny` is not applied as intended on Vitest's dev servers. Depending on the server, files that Vite refuses to serve by default (such as `.env`, private keys and certificates, `.npmrc`, and `.git`) or Vitest's own API token file (`.vitest-secret-token`) can be read over plain HTTP by a client that can reach the server. In Browser Mode with `test.projects`, a malicious website can also read `.env` values through the developer's browser.

This only applies when Vitest runs an HTTP server, which happens with the UI (`--ui`), Browser Mode, or `api` enabled. Plain `vitest` and `vitest run` don't listen on any port and are not affected. The fix ships in `vitest`, and `@vitest/ui` and `@vitest/browser` are listed because they are what enables the affected setups. Both pin `vitest` to the same version as a peer dependency, so upgrading either one also requires the patched `vitest`. Users who enable `api` without `@vitest/ui` or `@vitest/browser` are also affected and should upgrade `vitest`.

### Details

Vitest 5 adds its API token file to `server.fs.deny`, but neither server ended up with the intended list. That's because of two Vite behaviors. Vite applies its default deny list only when `server.fs.deny` is unset, and it compiles the list into a matcher during config resolution, so later changes to the array have no effect.

| plain `vitest` / `vitest run`      | none                            | not reachable            | not reachable                       |
| `--ui` or `api`                    | root                            | denied                   | **served** (fallback location only) |

findings.title: Vitest: Windows backslash traversal bypasses the @vitest/mocker redirect allowlist fix
findings.summary:
## Summary

The path traversal fix released for [GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9) can be bypassed on Windows by using a backslash in the redirect URL pathname.

The fixed code joins an attacker-controlled URL pathname with the Vite root using `node:path/posix`, then passes that string to Vite's file allowlist check. On Windows, a value such as `C:/project/root/..\secret.txt` retains `..\` during the POSIX join and begins with the allowed root, so the allowlist accepts it. The later `readFile()` call uses Windows filesystem semantics, where the backslash is a path separator, and reads the sibling file outside the configured root.

I reproduced the issue with the published `@vitest/mocker` packages in both fixed release lines:

- `@vitest/mocker@4.1.11`
- `@vitest/mocker@5.0.0`

The current `main` source at commit `2ce29d5fa758046e5453bd92b8ed6c9da9709bb5` has the same behavior.

## Patches

Fixed in `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Exposure of Sensitive Information via predictable export filenames
findings.summary:
## Summary

When a user exports content through `@apostrophecms/import-export`, the module copies the generated archive into uploadfs at `/exports/` and returns a public URL under `/uploads/exports/`. The filename is fully deterministic: site `shortName`, document type, a `YYYYMMDDHHmmss` timestamp, and the format extension. There is no secret token.

Anyone who can guess that path can download the archive with a normal unauthenticated HTTP GET while the file is still present (10 minutes by default, longer if the site raises `importExport.export.expiration`). That is a different model from attachment URLs, which rely on hard-to-guess IDs.

Sites that disable export, store uploads on a private backend with no anonymous read, or serve `/uploads` only behind authentication are not hit by the network download step—but the predictable naming is still a design flaw for the default local/public uploadfs layout.

Import-only workflows and imports themselves are out of scope; this is specific to the export download URL.

## Affected configurations

All of the following must apply:

1. The `@apostrophecms/import-export` module is enabled and export is allowed for at least one page or piece type, **and**
2. Export files are served the usual way: `copyIn` to `/exports/…` and delivery via the public `uploads` URL (default local uploadfs or any deployment that exposes the same path without per-file auth).

If export is turned off per type or globally, or `/uploads` is not world-readable, an anonymous attacker cannot pull the file over HTTP—but a co-resident attacker with filesystem or bucket listing access would still see guessable names.

## Remediation

- Put a high-entropy component in the export filename (e.g. `apos.util.generateId()`), **or**
- Stop publishing exports on a world-readable URL—serve downloads through an authenticated route and keep objects in a private prefix until then, **or**
- Document that `importExport.export.expiration` must stay short and treat `/upload

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken discloses existence of private/admin-only content to any authenticated user
findings.summary:
### Summary
The `slugTaken` endpoint returns a boolean indicating whether a slug is in use across
all document types and visibility levels, with no permission or type filter. Any logged-in
user (including editors) can enumerate the slug space of private pages, drafts, and
archived content.

### Details
`POST /api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken` with body `{ "slug": "target-slug" }` runs
a raw existence check against the documents collection. It does not:
- Check whether the requesting user has read permission for documents of that type.
- Filter by `visibility` (public, loginRequired, private).
- Filter by `viewRole`.
- Filter by publication status (draft vs published).

A single authenticated session can iterate the slug space to enumerate the full content
inventory of the CMS, including content the user is explicitly prohibited from viewing.

### PoC
```bash
# Any authenticated session works — editor role sufficient
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"known-private-page-slug"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": true }  — confirms private page exists

curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"slug":"zzz-nonexistent"}' \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/doc/slugTaken"
# → { "taken": false }
```

### Impact
Information disclosure. An attacker with any authenticated session can enumerate all
slugs in the system, mapping the full content structure of the CMS including private and
admin-only content.

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/:id bypasses viewRole restriction and exposes viewPermission-gated fields to lower-privileged users
findings.summary:
### Summary
The `getOne` REST endpoint for pages does not apply `viewRole` type-level restrictions
or `viewPermission` field-level redaction. An editor-level user who knows a document
`_id` can read the full content of admin-only pages and their privileged fields, while
the `getAll` endpoint correctly enforces both restrictions.

### Details
**Finding 3 — viewRole bypass:**
`modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js` exposes `getRestQuery(req, omitPermissionCheck =
false)`. The `getAll` path calls `publicApiCheckAsync` and threads the full query builder
pipeline including `viewRole` filtering. The `getOne` path uses a divergent code path
that skips this pipeline.

A page type declared with `viewRole: 'admin'` is inaccessible via `GET
/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage` (returns 403 to an editor) but is fully
returned by `GET /api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/:id:en:published` to the same editor.

**Finding 4 — viewPermission field leak:**
Fields decorated with `viewPermission: { action: 'edit', type: '@apostrophecms/page' }`
are stripped by `removeForbiddenFields` in the `getAll` path but are returned verbatim
in `getOne`. An editor who knows any document `_id` can read all
`viewPermission`-restricted fields.

### PoC
```bash
# Log in as editor, get session jar
EDITOR_JAR="..."

# getAll — correctly blocked
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page?type=secretPage"
# → 403 Forbidden

# getOne — bypassed, returns full document including viewPermission fields
curl -b "$EDITOR_JAR" \
  "http://TARGET/api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/ADMIN_PAGE_ID:en:published"
# → 200 OK, full doc including secretField value
```

### Impact
Editors can read the full content of any page — including those restricted to admins via
`viewRole` — if they know or can guess the `_id`. Sensitive field values gated by
`viewPermission` are also fully exposed. This breaks the content access control model
for any site using these decorators.

findings.title: ApostropheCMS sanitize-html: unbounded recursion when re-sanitizing the fallback of a discarded iframe (stack overflow, nestingLimit not enforced)
findings.summary:
### Summary

Since 2.18.0, when an `<iframe>` is not allowed and `disallowedTagsMode` is `'discard'` (the defaults),
its raw-text content is re-sanitized by a recursive call to `sanitizeHtml(text, options)` (the change
from #5564, fixing #5550). The recursion has no bound and starts each nested call with a fresh state.
Two consequences, both absent from 2.17.7 and 2.17.4:

1. A few kilobytes of unclosed `<iframe>` tags throw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
   with the default options. Any application that sanitizes untrusted HTML with 2.18.0 can be made to
   throw on a small crafted input.
2. `nestingLimit` is not enforced across a discarded iframe: each nested iframe restarts the depth
   count at zero, so the output can be nested arbitrarily deep regardless of the configured limit.

### Affected versions

- 2.18.0 (the current `latest`), and the `main` branch at the time of writing (the recursive call is
  still in `packages/sanitize-html/index.js`, in the `ontext` handler, branch
  `tag === 'iframe' && !tagAllowed(tag) && options.disallowedTagsMode === 'discard'`).
- Not affected: 2.17.7 and 2.17.4 (tested with the same inputs below).

Tested with Node.js v26.7.0.

### Reproduction 1: stack overflow with the default options

```js

// with 2.18.0:
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(1000));  // 8,000 chars: returns ''
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(2000));  // 16,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
sanitizeHtml('<iframe>'.repeat(20000)); // 160,000 chars: throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Results:

| input | 2.17.4 | 2.17.7 | 2.18.0 |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(1000)` | ok | ok | ok |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(2000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |
| `'<iframe>'.repeat(20000)` | ok | ok | RangeError |

The threshold depends on the remaining stack, so it is lower when `sanitizeHtml` is called from an
already deep call stack (for example inside a server-side

findings.title: virtualenv bash activate runs commands from an environment name with a backslash before $
findings.summary:
### Summary

The bash `activate` script escapes the environment name for only one of the two passes bash makes over `PS1`, so a
backslash in the name undoes the escaping and a name containing `\$(...)` runs as commands in the user's shell each
time bash draws the prompt.

### Affected area

`src/virtualenv/activation/bash/activate.sh`, the block that prepends the environment name to `PS1`.

### Attacker-controlled input

The environment name: the environment directory's name, or the `--prompt` or `VIRTUALENV_PROMPT` value. An attacker
needs to influence it, for example through a CI job or wrapper tool that passes a branch, project or job name through,
or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive. `--prompt .` takes the current directory's name.

### Details

bash handles `PS1` in two passes each time it draws the prompt: it first decodes backslash prompt escapes, turning `\\`
into `\` and `\$` into `$` (or `#` for root), and then runs parameter expansion, command substitution and arithmetic
expansion on the result. Since 21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in the name, but only
for the second pass, so the decode pass strips the escaping that a backslash in the name precedes. Releases before
21.13.0 do not escape the name at all. A bash running as root decodes `\$` to `#`, so the payload shows the wrong text
there but runs nothing. zsh does no decode pass and is not affected.

### Proof of concept

```console
$ virtualenv --prompt 'a\$(touch PWNED)' env
$ bash --norc --noprofile -c 'source env/bin/activate; printf "%s" "${PS1@P}"'
$ ls PWNED
PWNED
```

### Impact

Arbitrary command execution in the shell of a user who sources the `activate` script of an environment whose name an
attacker influenced, with that user's privileges, once per prompt draw.

### Versions tested

21.14.6 with bash 5.2.15 on Debian bookworm, as an unprivileged user and as root.

### Known mitigation

Set `VIRTUAL_ENV_DISABLE_PROMPT=1` before you sour

findings.title: Vite: Cross origin script execution through Vite custom middleware
findings.summary:
### Summary

When accessing a malicious site while a dev server using Vite is running, that site was able to load scripts in a page served by the dev server.

### Impact

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- the dev server passes an unchanged browser request URL to `server.transformIndexHtml`: this is normally used for `server.middlewareMode: true` or `appType: 'custom'`. The internal call for `appType: 'spa'` and `appType: 'mpa'` does not match this.
- the transformed HTML contains an inline module script
- from the script in the page served by the dev server, the app stores sensitive values in the location accessible or allows critical actions

### Details

[Vite's SSR guide for 8.2.1](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/421615865dad3ed39137d17281814fc78a41246c/docs/guide/ssr.md#L119-L131) documents the affected setup. The application embeds Vite in middleware mode, reads trusted HTML, and passes the browser's unchanged request URL to the transform:

```js
const url = req.originalUrl
template = await vite.transformIndexHtml(url, template)
```

For a development server at `http://localhost:5173`, an attacker can send this URL:

```text
http://localhost:5173//evil.example/payload.js?/../../package.json
```

In Vite 8.2.1, [`createDevHtmlTransformFn` and `getHtmlFilename` in `indexHtml.ts`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/421615865dad3ed39137d17281814fc78a41246c/packages/vite/src/node/server/middlewares/indexHtml.ts#L99-L115) use the request URL as both the transform `path` and the input to `path.join`. The value passed to `path.join` still includes its query text.

Chromium preserves `/../../package.json` because it follows `?` and is therefore query text. Vite treats the same characters as filesystem path components, so the `..` components resolve the derived filename to the existing project `package.json`.

[The existing file branch in `indexHtml.ts`](https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/421615865dad3ed39137d17281814fc78a41246c/package

findings.title: Vite: First 4 bytes of files outside of `server.fs` setting is exposed by `?vite-wasm-instance`
findings.summary:
### Summary

The first 4 bytes of files outside of `server.fs` setting can be returned to the browser by a request containing `?vite-wasm-instance`.

### Impact

 Only apps that match one of the following conditions are affected:

- explicitly expose the Vite dev server to the network using `--host` or the [`server.host`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options#server-host) option
- there's a file that has a sensitive information in **the first 4 bytes**
- uses Node.js or Deno to run Vite (if Bun is used, it is not affected)

### Details
Requests containing the `?vite-wasm-instance` query are handled by the internal Wasm plugin's `load` hook. The hook removes the query and reads the resulting path directly from disk, but the `server.fs` checks were not applied.

After reading the file, Vite attempts to parse it as WebAssembly. When that parse fails, Node and deno throws an error that contains the first 4 bytes of the file.

### PoC

Create a denied file and start an affected Vite dev server:

```bash
echo 'SECRET_KEY=abc123\n' > .env
npm run dev
curl 'http://localhost:5173/.env?vite-wasm-instance'
```

This will show
```
Failed to parse WASM file "<root>/.env": WebAssembly.compile(): expected magic word 00 61 73 6d, found 53 45 43 52 @+0
```

findings.title: virtualenv activate runs commands from the environment name in zsh with PROMPT_SUBST
findings.summary:
### Impact

zsh users activate an environment with the bash `activate` script, which puts the environment name into `PS1`. Since
21.13.0 the script escapes backslashes, dollar signs and backticks in that name, but only when `BASH_VERSION` is set, so
zsh gets the raw value. With the `PROMPT_SUBST` option set, zsh runs parameter expansion, command substitution and
arithmetic expansion on `PS1` each time it draws the prompt. A name that contains `$(...)`, backticks or `${...}` then
runs as commands in the user's shell, once per prompt.

The name comes from the environment directory, or from `--prompt` or `VIRTUALENV_PROMPT`. After you create an
environment with:

```console
$ virtualenv 'x$(touch PWNED)y'
```

`source 'x$(touch PWNED)y/bin/activate'` in a zsh session with `PROMPT_SUBST` set creates `PWNED`, and the prompt shows
`(xy)`. Passing that value as `--prompt` to an environment with a plain name has the same effect. Without
`PROMPT_SUBST`, zsh shows the name as text and runs nothing. bash runs nothing either.

A plain zsh starts with `PROMPT_SUBST` off. oh-my-zsh users have it on: oh-my-zsh loads
[`lib/theme-and-appearance.zsh`](https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/blob/4d4cfc287e9d887b81242c0e431b5f49f9cec5c1/lib/theme-and-appearance.zsh#L5)
at startup, and that file sets it. An attacker needs to influence the environment path or prompt: a CI job or wrapper
tool that passes a branch, project or job name through, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive.
`--prompt .` takes the current directory's name.

though without running commands.

The bug is in releases up to and including 21.14.3. The payload runs on 20.26.6 and 21.14.3, and the reporter confirmed
21.9.1.

### Patches

Fixed in 21.14.4. Under zsh, `activate` now escapes the name the way it does under bash and doubles
`%`, so the example above runs nothing and the prompt sh

findings.title: virtualenv activation scripts run code from a path that contains a placeholder name
findings.summary:
### Impact

`ViaTemplateActivator.instantiate_template` replaces the placeholders in an activation template one key at a time, each across the whole text. When a value that it already substituted and quoted contains the name of a later placeholder, the later pass rewrites that name inside the quoted literal. The inserted value brings its own quotes, which close the outer literal, and the rest of the path runs as code when a user activates the environment.

`__VIRTUAL_NAME__` holds the environment's directory name, so a destination such as `A__VIRTUAL_NAME__B/x'$(touch PWNED)'y` is enough. In the default `activate` for bash, the `VIRTUAL_ENV` line renders as:

```sh
VIRTUAL_ENV='/tmp/t/A'x'"'"'$(touch PWNED)'"'"'y'B/x'"'"'$(touch PWNED)'"'"'y'
```

Sourcing that script runs `touch PWNED`. The same payload in a path without the placeholder name runs nothing. `activate.fish` runs the command the same way, and the reporter also showed Python code execution through `activate.xsh` and `bin/activate_this.py`. In `activate.csh`, a directory named after a prompt display placeholder, such as `__VIRTUAL_PROMPT_DISPLAY_TCSH__`, breaks the script with `Unmatched '''`.

No change to `quote()` can stop this, because the rewrite happens after `quote()` ran; it defeats `shlex.quote` and `repr()` alike.

An attacker needs to influence the destination path or `--prompt`: a CI job or wrapper tool that builds the path from a branch or project name, or a directory in a cloned repository or unpacked archive.

The bug affects versions 20.26.6 through 21.14.1. Version 20.26.6 first quoted template values (#2768) and introduced the per-key loop.

### Patches

Fixed in 21.14.2. Activation scripts now keep a placeholder name in the environment's path or prompt as plain text, and activating the example above runs nothing. Fix: https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/602b26623a724827ff171bf11fef4ad186d01f74

### Workarounds

Do not create an environment whose path or `--prompt` contains a plac

findings.title: Slack Morphism verifier errors disclose valid HMACs in the logs
findings.summary:
### Summary

Slack Morphism exposes the correct Slack request HMAC when signature verification fails.

For an invalid request, `slack-morphism` computes the correct signature for the attacker-controlled timestamp and request body and stores it in `SlackEventWrongSignatureError.generated_hash`. The error's `Debug` and `Display` representations expose that value, and the default Axum listener error handler logs it at error level.

An attacker who can both reach the application's Slack callback endpoint and read its application/service logs can therefore use the verifier as a chosen-message HMAC oracle. The attacker can send an arbitrary request with an invalid signature, recover the correct signature from the resulting log entry, and resend the same request within the five-minute freshness window. The second request passes Slack Morphism's signature verification and reaches the protected application callback without the attacker knowing the Slack signing secret.

I reproduced this end-to-end against both the Axum and Hyper integrations in `slack-morphism` 2.26.0 and 2.27.0.

### Details

The vulnerability is in Slack Morphism's request signature verification error path.

In `src/signature_verifier.rs`, `SlackEventSignatureVerifier::verify` computes the expected signature before comparing it with the untrusted `X-Slack-Signature` supplied by the request.

On a mismatch, the implementation creates a `SlackEventWrongSignatureError` containing the complete correct signature in its public `generated_hash` field.

Relevant source path:

```text
src/signature_verifier.rs:46-59
```

The error type is defined around:

```text
src/signature_verifier.rs:182-199
```

`generated_hash` is a public `String`; the type derives `Debug`, and its `Display` implementation also prints the generated signature.

The resulting source-to-sink path is:

1. `SlackEventSignatureVerifier::verify` computes the expected HMAC for the attacker-controlled timestamp and raw request body.

findings.title: OpenChoreo: Authorization bypass on WorkflowRun update allows cross-project takeover of workflow runs
findings.summary:
## Summary

The OpenChoreo API server authorized `PUT .../workflowruns/{runName}` against ownership metadata taken from the request body, while the object it actually mutated was selected by the URL path. Nothing forced the two to agree.

A `WorkflowRun`'s membership in a project and component is carried entirely by its `openchoreo.dev/project` and `openchoreo.dev/component` labels. Because the `workflowrun:update` check read those labels from the submitted object rather than the stored one, a caller holding `workflowrun:update` on one component could name a run belonging to a different project or component in the URL, supply labels for the component they legitimately control, pass the check, and have the unrelated run rewritten with their own ownership labels.

The namespace is taken from the URL and feeds both the authorization check and the Kubernetes read, so it cannot diverge. This is cross-project and cross-component escalation inside a single namespace, not a cross-tenant issue.

## Impact

Rewriting the ownership labels transfers authority over the run. Every other WorkflowRun check (view, logs, events, status, delete, list) derives its scope from the stored labels, so once the write lands the policy engine legitimately grants the attacker access to an object they never had rights to. They can then:

- Read the victim's build logs. These stream raw pod logs from the workflow plane and routinely carry source paths, registry destinations, and credentials a build step echoed by accident.
- Read the run's Kubernetes events.
- Delete the run.

So the primary impact is confidentiality and availability, not only integrity. On the integrity side, `spec.workflow.parameters` can be overwritten on a pending run, and manipulating the two ownership labels can either wedge the run in a permanent `ComponentValidationFailed` condition or downgrade it to a standalone run that skips component validation.

Exploitation requires an authenticated caller with an `AuthzRoleBinding

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Unauthenticated resource exhaustion via pre-auth aposBigUpload processing in @apostrophecms/import-export
findings.summary:
## Summary

A potential unauthenticated denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the chunked import upload path used by `@apostrophecms/import-export`.

The affected import API routes invoke:

`self.apos.http.bigUploadMiddleware()`

before the actual import handler performs its authentication check.

Because no `authorize` callback is supplied to `bigUploadMiddleware()`, unauthenticated requests can reach the `aposBigUpload` `start`, `chunk`, and `end` operations before the later `req.user` check rejects the import.

As a result, an unauthenticated remote attacker can create server-side upload state, write chunk data to upload storage, trigger temporary-file processing, and cause attacker-controlled cleanup operations before authentication is enforced.

## Affected Component

Package:

`@apostrophecms/import-export`

Confirmed affected version:

`3.6.2`

Potential earlier affected versions:

The issue may affect earlier 3.x releases in which the current big-upload-based import implementation is present. I have not yet fully verified the exact introduction version and recommend that the maintainers confirm the affected version range.

## Vulnerability Type

Primary:

**CWE-400 — Uncontrolled Resource Consumption**

Related:

**CWE-306 — Missing Authentication for Critical Function**

**CWE-770 — Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling**

## Technical Details

The page import route registers the following middleware chain:

`packages/import-export/modules/@apostrophecms/import-export-page/index.js`

```javascript
importExportImport: [
  self.apos.http.bigUploadMiddleware(),
  async (req) => {
    return self.apos.modules['@apostrophecms/import-export']
      .import(req, self.__meta.name);
  }
]
```

No `authorize` callback is passed to `bigUploadMiddleware()`.

The `bigUploadMiddleware()` implementation explicitly supports an `authorize` callback and performs that authorization before processing the `aposBigUpload` protocol when supplied.

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ). Implementing the DNS parser in Rust offers
